**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. Web search query: “Conti ransomware as a service structure leaks internal organization aliases law enforcement indictment sanctions official”
2. Web search query: “Conti ransomware original leaks internal chats analysis affiliates management negotiation”
3. Web search query: “site:justice.gov Conti ransomware indictment alias”
4. Web search query: “site:treasury.gov Conti ransomware sanctions”
5. Web search query: “Conti indictment Maksim Galochkin Rudenskiy Tsarev Zhuykov Lytvynenko aliases official DOJ”
6. Web search query: “Conti ransomware sanctions aliases Target Reshaev Professor Tramp Dandis official”
7. Web search query: “Conti Wizard Spider law enforcement attribution official report”
8. Web search query: “Krebs Conti leaks internal organization coders testers administrators aliases negotiation chats”
9. Web search query: “Conti leaks internal chats roles hierarchy affiliates recruitment salaries infrastructure analysis”

The benchmark-returned corpus contained four unique URLs, identified below as SRC-001 through SRC-004. The later searches returned the same four benchmark sources and did not add a separate indictment, sanctions, court filing, or primary leak URL.

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

### Scope and evidence limitations

- The available benchmark corpus consists of:
  - One official U.S. government Rewards for Justice page.
  - One official U.S. Department of Justice case page.
  - Two secondary analyses of the Conti leaks and Conti’s operations.
- The returned excerpts do not include the full text of the original Conti internal chats, the Conti manual, the underlying indictments, the linked DOJ press releases, or any separate Treasury sanctions notice.
- The Rapid7 source states that some leaked messages were encrypted and could not be read, so “the information provided is necessarily incomplete.” [2]
- Rapid7 also states that it did not access data requiring use of remote-server credentials or usernames and passwords, and “strongly recommend[s] against doing so.” [2]
- The available evidence does not establish a complete mapping between Conti aliases and legal identities.
- The available evidence does not establish that any of the five individuals named on the DOJ page correspond to the five aliases identified by Rewards for Justice.
- The DOJ page expressly states that charged defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. [4]

### Evidence table

| No. | Subject | Classification | Evidence and precise source statement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Conti’s organizational identity | Official assessment | Rewards for Justice characterizes “Conti (also known as Wizard Spider)” as “a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure.” [1] |
| 2 | Conti’s first detection | Official statement | Rewards for Justice states: “First detected in 2019.” [1] |
| 3 | Conti’s operational scale | Official statement | Rewards for Justice states that Conti ransomware “has been used to conduct more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure.” [1] |
| 4 | Conti victims | Official statement | Rewards for Justice identifies targets including “law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities.” It states that healthcare and first-responder networks were among “more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, over 290 of which are located in the United States.” [1] |
| 5 | Conti’s extortion workflow | Official characterization | Rewards for Justice states: “Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim.” [1] |
| 6 | Negotiation and payment process | Official characterization | Rewards for Justice states: “The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction.” [1] |
| 7 | Double extortion | Reported secondary finding | CIS Security describes Conti as “a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up.” [3] |
| 8 | Publication or sale of stolen data | Official characterization | Rewards for Justice states: “If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by the Conti actors.” [1] |
| 9 | Ransom amounts | Official statement | Rewards for Justice states: “Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands being as high as $25 million.” [1] |
| 10 | RaaS business model generally | Secondary contextual explanation | CIS Security states that the shift toward RaaS has involved groups leasing malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with developers, “often in a 70-30 split.” [3] This is presented as a general RaaS model and is not expressly stated in the returned excerpt to be Conti’s exact profit split. |
| 11 | Conti’s business character | Secondary leak analysis | Rapid7’s article includes the heading “Conti is a business – and a well-funded one.” [2] It states that much of the discussion in the chat logs concerned “fairly mundane” business matters, although the returned excerpt truncates the remainder of that discussion. |
| 12 | Source and timing of the Conti leaks | Reported fact | Rapid7 states that on February 27, 2022, Twitter user “@ContiLeaks” released “a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti.” [2] |
| 13 | Political dispute within Conti | Reported fact | Rapid7 states that, before the chat disclosures, Conti pledged support for the Russian government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine; “a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization.” [2] |
| 14 | Conti’s revised public statement | Reported fact | Rapid7 states that two days later Conti posted a second message revising its statement “to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted.” [2] |
| 15 | Size and format of the leaked chat archive | Reported fact | Rapid7 states that a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the AnonFiles website and contained “14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files.” [2] |
| 16 | Incomplete nature of the leak | Documented limitation | Rapid7 states: “However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete.” [2] |
| 17 | Content of the leaked materials | Reported fact | Rapid7 states that the remaining files contained “internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes.” [2] |
| 18 | Additional leak materials | Reported fact | Rapid7 states that on February 28 and March 1, additional files were posted, along with “a number of pro-Ukraine tweets.” [2] |
| 19 | Credentials and infrastructure exposed in the leak | Reported fact | Rapid7 states that the leaked materials included “a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts.” It also states that @ContiLeaks shared access details for “a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files.” [2] |
| 20 | Non-access to exposed systems | Documented limitation | Rapid7 states: “However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so.” [2] |
| 21 | Alleged ransomware source code | Reported claim | Rapid7 states that @ContiLeaks shared a file that they “purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware” but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” [2] |
| 22 | Alleged developer disclosure | Reported claim | Rapid7 states that @ContiLeaks named “one alleged Conti developer,” providing that person’s email address and GitHub account. The returned excerpt does not provide the developer’s name, email address, or GitHub identity. [2] |
| 23 | Identity of the leaker | Inference / unresolved uncertainty | Rapid7 states that the scale of the leaked information “suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates.” This is an assessment, not an established identity. [2] |
| 24 | Conti’s internal business units | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security reports that Conti’s handlers “divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets.” [3] |
| 25 | Coders | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that Conti hired programmers as “Coders” to “write malicious code and integrate different technologies.” [3] |
| 26 | Testers | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that Conti relied on “Testers” to “validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies.” [3] |
| 27 | Other internal roles | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that Conti also had “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers” working internally. [3] |
| 28 | Outsourced spamming | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that “spamming functions [were] contracted outside the organization.” [3] |
| 29 | Department budgets | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states: “Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another.” [3] |
| 30 | Number of employees | Reported claim based on an insider | CIS Security states: “According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021.” [3] |
| 31 | Staff turnover and dismissals | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that the employee number “didn't remain consistent,” because Conti “sometimes let people go following internal security breaches.” [3] |
| 32 | Investment in Cobalt Strike | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that Conti allocated “$60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool.” [3] |
| 33 | Security and antivirus testing expenses | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that Conti budgeted “several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the ‘Testers’ could use for their evaluations.” [3] |
| 34 | Reverse-engineering priorities | Secondary analysis of leak materials | CIS Security states that Conti redefined the focus of its “Reverse Engineers” in July 2021 “to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time.” [3] |
| 35 | Conti’s relationship with other malware groups | Secondary reported assessment | CIS Security states that Conti “also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot.” [3] |
| 36 | Associated malware and tools | Official source listing | Rewards for Justice lists the associated cyberthreat organization as “Conti” and “Wizard Spider.” It lists associated malicious cyber applications as “Conti ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS),” “TrickBot,” “IcedID,” “Cobalt Strike,” and “ZLoader.” [1] |
| 37 | Conti’s political positioning after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine | Official statement | Rewards for Justice states: “After Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government.” [1] |
| 38 | Government-linked characterization | Official assessment | Rewards for Justice offers a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons who, while “acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government,” participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. On the same page, it states that Conti is “Russian government-linked.” [1] |
| 39 | Aliases publicly identified by the U.S. government | Official assessment / unresolved identity | Rewards for Justice states that malicious cyber actors known by the online aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are “believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group.” [1] |
| 40 | Alias-to-organization association | Official listing | The Rewards for Justice page lists the “Associated Cyberthreat Organization” as “Conti” and “Wizard Spider” for the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis.” [1] |
| 41 | Location associated with the aliases | Official listing | Rewards for Justice lists “Russia” under “Associated Location(s)” for the Conti-linked actors. [1] |
| 42 | Legal identities connected to Conti activity | Official DOJ record | The DOJ Middle District of Tennessee Conti page identifies Case Number `3:23-CR-00092` and defendants “Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov.” [4] |
| 43 | Charges against four defendants | Official DOJ record / allegation | The DOJ page states that, on September 7, 2023, “for their roles in the Conti ransomware conspiracy,” Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov were charged with “conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.” [4] |
| 44 | Presumption of innocence for four defendants | Official legal qualification | The DOJ page states: “All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.” [4] |
| 45 | Additional defendant and case number | Official DOJ record | The DOJ page identifies Case Number `3:23-CR-00088` and defendant “Oleksii Lytvynenko.” [4] |
| 46 | Charge involving Oleksii Lytvynenko | Official DOJ record / allegation | The DOJ page states that, on November 7, 2025, “for his role in the Conti ransomware conspiracy,” Oleksii Lytvynenko was charged with “conspiracy to deploy Conti, a ransomware variant that infected victim computers and networks, encrypting their data.” [4] |
| 47 | Guilty plea by Oleksii Lytvynenko | Official DOJ record | The DOJ page states that on June 10, 2026, Oleksii Lytvynenko “entered a plea of guilty to Count 2 of the indictment, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement with the United States.” [4] |
| 48 | Sentencing schedule | Official DOJ record | The DOJ page states that Lytvynenko was scheduled to be sentenced on September 10, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. [4] |
| 49 | Victim restitution process | Official DOJ record | The DOJ page states that victims could provide restitution requests and supporting documents to the U.S. Attorney’s Office in advance of sentencing using the Victim Impact Statement form. [4] |
| 50 | Overall victim count in the DOJ case description | Official DOJ statement | The DOJ page states: “Conti ransomware was a malicious software that affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world.” [4] |
| 51 | Victim notification and rights | Official DOJ statement | The DOJ page states that after a defendant is charged with a federal crime, victims are entitled to be notified of public court proceedings. It also identifies federal crime-victim rights under the Justice for All Act of 2004, 18 U.S.C. §3771. [4] |
| 52 | Victim impact statements | Official DOJ statement | The DOJ page states that victims may submit Victim Impact Statements explaining the physical, emotional, and/or financial effects of the crime; those statements may assist the court in deciding the sentence and whether restitution should be ordered. Victims also have the right to speak at sentencing. [4] |
| 53 | Operational disruption after the leak | Secondary technical assessment | Rapid7 states that, as of March 2, 2022, Conti began taking down exposed infrastructure as a result of the chat disclosure. Rapid7 assessed that, because of Conti’s “sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021,” it remained “an active and significant threat.” [2] |
| 54 | Resumption of operations | Secondary technical observation | Rapid7 states: “As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti.” [2] |
| 55 | Subsequent dismantling and rebranding | Secondary reported account | CIS Security states that, in the months after the leaks, Conti’s handlers began dismantling their operations. It reports that in May 2022 Bleeping Computer wrote that “the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members.” [3] |
| 56 | Shutdown of leak and negotiation infrastructure | Secondary reported account | CIS Security states that approximately one month after the reported rebranding, “the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure.” [3] |
| 57 | Conflicting or sequential operational assessments | Unresolved chronology / apparent tension | Rapid7 reported observed “resumption of normal operations from Conti” as of March 9, 2022. CIS Security later reported that the larger platform shut down and rebranded into smaller units in May 2022, followed approximately one month later by the shutdown of data-leak and negotiation infrastructure. These statements can describe different stages or components of Conti’s activity, but the returned sources do not reconcile them. [2][3] |
| 58 | Internal hierarchy | Inference from organizational evidence | The division into business units, distinct specialist roles, separate budgets, cross-unit borrowing, staffing decisions, and operational coordination supports an inference that Conti had an organized internal management structure rather than being only a loose collection of independent actors. The returned sources do not provide a complete named hierarchy or identify a definitive leader. [2][3] |
| 59 | Management and business administration | Inference from leak analysis | The reported existence of administrators, departmental budgets, employee dismissals, recruitment or staffing decisions, tool purchases, testing budgets, and negotiators or negotiation infrastructure supports an inference that Conti operated with business-administration functions. CIS Security describes broader cybercrime commercialization as involving “HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment,” but the returned excerpt does not attribute every one of those functions specifically to Conti. [3] |
| 60 | Affiliates and outsourcing | Documented in part; unresolved in detail | CIS Security describes a RaaS model in which affiliates conduct intrusions and share profits with developers, and states that Conti contracted out spamming functions. Rapid7 suggests the leak may have come from “a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates.” The available sources do not identify individual affiliates, specify the exact Conti affiliate contract, or establish the identities of the alleged affiliates. [2][3] |
| 61 | Malware development workflow | Secondary analysis of leak materials | The reported “Coders,” “Reverse Engineers,” “Testers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers,” together with the Cobalt Strike purchase, antivirus-testing budget, and Windows 11 focus, document or support a workflow involving malware development, integration, testing against security tools, penetration testing, and platform adaptation. [3] |
| 62 | Negotiation workflow | Official and secondary evidence | Rewards for Justice documents ransom letters directing victims to an online portal and publication or sale of stolen data if payment is not made. CIS Security reports that Conti later shut down its “negotiation infrastructure.” Together, these sources document a payment-negotiation and data-leak workflow, but do not identify individual negotiators or provide the internal negotiation rules. [1][3] |
| 63 | Victim targeting | Official statement | The official source identifies U.S. and Western critical infrastructure, law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, municipalities, healthcare networks, and first-responder networks among Conti’s targets or victims. [1] |
| 64 | Public attribution to Wizard Spider | Official assessment | Rewards for Justice explicitly identifies Conti as “also known as Wizard Spider.” [1] |
| 65 | Public attribution to Russia | Official assessment and reported leak context | Rewards for Justice characterizes Conti as Russian government-linked and associates the listed aliases with Russia. Rapid7 and CIS Security report Conti’s public support statement for Russia following the invasion of Ukraine. These are official and secondary assessments or reports, not a complete public proof of the legal identities or command relationships of all Conti personnel. [1][2][3] |
| 66 | Named individuals versus aliases | Unresolved uncertainty | The official sources separately identify five aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—and five legal names—Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko. The returned corpus does not state that any particular alias corresponds to any particular named defendant. [1][4] |
| 67 | Charges versus adjudicated guilt | Legal limitation | The DOJ record documents charges against four defendants and a guilty plea by Lytvynenko to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud. It does not, in the returned excerpt, provide judgments or convictions for Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, or Zhuykov. [4] |
| 68 | Sanctions evidence | Missing from returned corpus | The searches sought Treasury sanctions and related official records, but the returned benchmark corpus contains no separate Treasury sanctions URL or sanctions notice. No sanctions finding should be inferred from the available sources. |
| 69 | Complete identity attribution | Missing / unresolved | The returned corpus does not provide a complete list of Conti personnel, a definitive leadership roster, a complete alias-to-name mapping, or a fully documented relationship between Conti’s internal roles and the defendants named in the DOJ case. |
| 70 | Original leak provenance | Reported fact with uncertainty | The leak was publicly released by the Twitter account @ContiLeaks. Rapid7 states that the scale of the material suggests the leaker was likely a very senior member or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates, but this remains an inference and not a proven identity. [2] |

### Concise synthesis by evidentiary category

#### (a) Directly documented

- An official U.S. government source calls Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, a Russian government-linked RaaS group. [1]
- The same source identifies the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as believed to be linked to Conti. [1]
- The official source describes Conti’s operating method as stealing files, encrypting servers and workstations, demanding payment through an online portal, and selling or publishing stolen data when payment is not made. [1]
- The official source reports more than 1,000 ransomware operations, more than 400 worldwide victim organizations, and more than 290 U.S. victims among the specified healthcare and first-responder networks. [1]
- DOJ publicly identifies the defendants Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko in Conti-related cases. [4]
- DOJ documents charges against the first four defendants for conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. [4]
- DOJ documents Lytvynenko’s charge involving conspiracy to deploy Conti and his June 10, 2026 guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud. [4]
- The leak archive contained 14 megabytes across 393 JSON files, although some messages were encrypted and unreadable. [2]
- Secondary leak analyses report internal roles including Coders, Testers, Administrators, Reverse Engineers, and Penetration Testers/Hackers; externally contracted spamming; separate budgets; and more than 60 employees in July 2021 according to an insider. [3]
- Secondary analysis reports a $60,000 Cobalt Strike purchase, monthly security and antivirus testing expenses, and a Windows 11 focus for Reverse Engineers. [3]

#### (b) Alleged or assessed

- The U.S. government’s characterization of Conti as Russian government-linked is an official assessment. [1]
- The association of the five aliases with Conti is stated as “believed to be linked,” not as a final judicial finding. [1]
- The alleged source code, alleged developer, alleged command-and-control servers, and alleged storage servers came from materials shared by @ContiLeaks and are described with qualifications by Rapid7. [2]
- Conti’s apparent ties to TrickBot are presented by CIS Security as an appearance or reported relationship, not as a fully documented legal finding. [3]
- The precise RaaS profit split of “often in a 70-30 split” is a general contextual description of RaaS and is not expressly established by the returned excerpt as Conti’s exact split. [3]

#### (c) Inferred from multiple sources

- Conti appears to have operated as a commercially organized enterprise with internal departments, specialist roles, budgets, software acquisition, testing, staffing decisions, affiliate relationships, extortion infrastructure, and negotiation functions. [1][2][3]
- The combination of stolen-data exfiltration, encryption, online negotiation, payment demands, and publication or sale of data supports a multi-stage double-extortion workflow. [1][3]
- The role structure and technical budgets support an inference that Conti maintained an internal malware-development and quality-assurance process. [3]
- The leak scale supports Rapid7’s inference that the leaker was probably a senior member or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates, but does not prove which. [2]
- The March 2022 operational resumption reported by Rapid7 and the later May–June 2022 shutdown/rebranding reported by CIS Security may represent successive stages or different components of Conti’s activity. The sources do not reconcile the chronology. [2][3]

#### (d) Remaining unknown

- The identities of “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are not supplied. [1]
- The corpus does not connect those aliases to Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, or Oleksii Lytvynenko. [1][4]
- The corpus does not provide a complete Conti hierarchy, definitive leadership identities, or a full list of employees and affiliates.
- The corpus does not provide the exact Conti affiliate revenue split, affiliate contracts, recruitment records, or named recruiters.
- The corpus does not provide the full original chat archive or the complete Conti manual.
- The corpus does not provide a separate Treasury sanctions record.
- The corpus does not provide the complete factual allegations in the indictments or the linked DOJ press releases.
- The corpus does not establish convictions or final adjudications for Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, or Zhuykov.
- The corpus does not establish whether the individuals charged in the DOJ cases were administrators, developers, affiliates, negotiators, infrastructure operators, or other specific internal-role categories.
- The corpus does not resolve whether Conti’s later rebranded units were legally or operationally continuous with the original Conti organization.
- The corpus does not fully reconcile the public attribution of Conti to Russian government-linked activity with the internal political disagreement reported in the leak materials, including members who sided with Ukraine. [1][2]

---

### Sources

[1] **Conti – Rewards For Justice** — official U.S. government Rewards for Justice page; publication date not stated in the returned excerpt; page displays © 2026.  
https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/

[2] **Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict** — Rapid7 threat-research blog, March 1, 2022; last updated May 9, 2024.  
https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/

[3] **The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization** — Center for Internet Security secondary analysis; publication date not stated in the returned excerpt.  
https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization

[4] **Conti Ransomware** — U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, official case page; updated July 8, 2026.  
https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2
